reference.source: Cardiology and congenital heart disease references
clinicalPearls: An aneurysm of an aortic sinus that ruptures, usually into a right-sided chamber, creating an aorto-cardiac shunt
The right coronary sinus is most commonly involved, often rupturing into the right ventricle or atrium
Rupture may be acute with chest pain, breathlessness and heart failure, or more insidious
It produces a loud continuous murmur from the aorto-cardiac shunt
It may be congenital or associated with connective tissue disease, infection or trauma
Diagnosis is by echocardiography and surgical or transcatheter closure is usually required
reference.pathophysiology: A sinus of Valsalva aneurysm is a localised dilatation of an aortic sinus, typically from congenital weakness at the junction of the aortic media and the annulus, sometimes exacerbated by connective tissue disease or infection. When it ruptures, high-pressure aortic blood flows through the defect into a lower-pressure cardiac chamber, most often the right ventricle or atrium, creating a left-to-right (aorto-cardiac) shunt. The resulting volume load causes heart failure, and the continuous pressure gradient generates a characteristic continuous murmur.
additionalDifferentials: Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation
additionalInvestigations: Cardiac CT or MRI to define the aneurysm and rupture site
Assessment of shunt magnitude and cardiac function
Evaluation for associated ventricular septal defect and aortic regurgitation
redFlags: Acute heart failure or haemodynamic collapse at rupture
Compression of adjacent structures or coronary compromise by an unruptured aneurysm
reference.prognosis: Untreated rupture leads to progressive heart failure, but surgical or transcatheter closure generally gives good results, particularly when performed before severe ventricular dysfunction develops.
pitfalls: Attributing the continuous murmur to a patent ductus or coronary fistula
Missing an associated ventricular septal defect or aortic regurgitation
Delaying closure until heart failure is advanced
management: Definitive closure of the ruptured defect by surgical patch repair or transcatheter device occlusion of the aorto-cardiac fistula
Concurrent repair of associated lesions at operation, including closure of a coexisting ventricular septal defect and aortic valve repair or replacement for significant aortic regurgitation
Medical stabilisation of the volume-loaded heart failure with diuretics and afterload reduction while awaiting definitive intervention
Urgent management of acute decompensation or cardiogenic shock, expediting emergency closure when haemodynamic collapse occurs
Assessment for and treatment of infective endocarditis where the aneurysm is infection-related, with appropriate antimicrobial cover
Serial echocardiographic surveillance for residual shunt, ventricular function and progression of aortic regurgitation after closure
Early referral to a combined cardiology and cardiac surgery team for closure before severe ventricular dysfunction develops
